terms.def: A method that claims more of an asset's cost as depreciation in its early years, reducing taxable profit sooner.
The rules a business uses to decide when income and expenses are recorded, usually cash or accrual accounting.
The span of time a set of financial statements covers, such as a month, quarter or year.
Software that records transactions, reconciles bank accounts and produces reports, such as Xero, MYOB or QuickBooks.
Money your business owes to suppliers for goods and services it has received but not yet paid for.
Money owed to your business by customers for goods or services already delivered.
How many times a year a business collects its average accounts receivable. A higher number means customers pay faster.
Recording income when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, regardless of when cash changes hands.
What an asset cost you for tax purposes, including purchase price and certain costs of buying, holding and selling it. Used to work out a capital gain or loss.

US.def: An asset's cost for tax purposes, adjusted for improvements and depreciation. Used to work out a gain or loss when you sell.

CA.def: An asset's cost for tax purposes, including purchase costs and adjustments. Used to work out a capital gain or loss when you sell.

terms.def: Your total income minus specific adjustments, used by the IRS to work out your tax and eligibility for many credits.
Specific deductions, such as some retirement contributions, that reduce gross income before adjusted gross income is calculated.
A cost that a contract allows you to bill to the customer.
A tax return {lodged} again with corrections after the original was submitted to {tax_authority}.
Spreading the cost of an intangible asset, or the repayment of a loan, over a set period.
A loan repaid in regular scheduled instalments that cover both interest and principal.
The interest rate earned or charged over a year once compounding is taken into account.
An increase in the value of an asset over time.
{tax_authority_short}'s calculation of the tax you owe after you {lodge} a return. The term is also used for the value given to a property for rates or property tax.
How an investment portfolio is divided between asset classes such as shares, property, bonds and cash.
A bankruptcy in which the debtor has assets that can be sold to repay creditors.
Anything a person or business owns that has a monetary value.
An independent examination of financial records, or a review by {tax_authority} to check that tax has been reported correctly.
Total tax paid divided by taxable income, shown as a percentage.
A financial statement showing what a business owns (assets), owes (liabilities) and the owners' equity at a point in time.
Matching the transactions in your accounting records with your bank statement and explaining any differences.
A legal process for people or businesses that cannot pay their debts, under which some debts may be released.
The level of sales at which total revenue equals total fixed and variable costs, so the business makes neither a profit nor a loss.
The money and other financial resources used to start, run and grow a business.
The profit made when an asset, such as property or shares, is sold for more than its cost.
Tax on the capital gain made when you sell certain assets, such as investment property or shares.

NZ.def: A rule that taxes the gain on residential property sold within a set period after purchase. New Zealand has no general capital gains tax.

US.def: Federal (and often state) tax on gains from selling assets. Rates depend on whether the asset was held short or long term.

terms.def: The loss made when an asset is sold for less than its cost. It can often be used to reduce capital gains.
Recording income when money is received and expenses when they are paid.
A financial report showing where cash came from and where it went over a period.
The list of all the accounts in a business's general ledger, used to categorise every transaction.
The direct costs of producing or buying the goods a business sold, such as materials and direct labour.
The tax payable on income earned in the current tax year.
Combining several debts into one loan, ideally at a lower interest rate or with simpler repayments.
How much of a person's income goes towards repaying debt. Lenders use it to assess borrowing capacity.
An expense you can subtract from your assessable income to reduce the tax you pay.

US.def: An expense you can subtract from your income to reduce the tax you pay.

CA.def: An expense you can subtract from your income to reduce the tax you pay.

terms.def: A person, such as a child, who relies on someone else for financial support.
Spreading the cost of a business asset over its useful life, recognising the fall in its value.
A tax paid directly to the government by the person or business it is charged on, such as income tax.
A distribution of a company's profits to its shareholders.
A thorough review of a business or investment before buying it, to understand its value and risks.
Buying and selling goods or services online.
Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation: a measure of operating performance.

US.def: Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization: a measure of operating performance.

CA.def: Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization: a measure of operating performance.

terms.def: Money set aside to cover unexpected expenses, such as repairs or a drop in income.
The value of an asset after the debts secured against it are subtracted. In a business, the owners' share of its assets.
Everything a person owns, minus what they owe, particularly when they die.
Regular payments made during the year towards your expected income tax, so you don't face one large bill after you {lodge} your return.
A tax on specific goods such as fuel, alcohol and tobacco, usually charged per unit rather than on price.
The price an asset would sell for between a willing buyer and a willing seller in an open market.
A formal report of a business's financial activities and position, such as the profit and loss, balance sheet and cash flow statement.
The 12-month period a business uses for accounting and tax reporting.
Long-term physical assets a business owns and uses to earn income, such as equipment, vehicles and buildings.
A tax system in which everyone pays the same rate regardless of income.
Several people each owning a share of an asset, such as a property, and sharing its costs and benefits.
Credits for the company tax already paid on a dividend. Shareholders can use them to reduce their own tax.

NZ.def: Credits for the company tax already paid on a dividend. Shareholders can use them to reduce their own tax.

terms.def: Tax employers pay on certain non-cash benefits given to employees, such as a car or paid expenses.

UK.def: Non-cash benefits given to employees, such as a company car, which are taxable and reported to HMRC.

IE.def: Non-cash benefits given to employees, such as a company car, which are taxed through payroll.

US.def: Non-cash benefits given to employees. Many are taxable as wages unless a specific exclusion applies.

CA.def: Non-cash benefits given to employees, such as a company car, which are included in their employment income.

terms.def: A loan to the government that pays a fixed rate of interest until it matures.
Total income before any tax or deductions are taken out.
Revenue minus the cost of goods sold. It shows how much a business makes on what it sells, before overheads.
Gross profit as a percentage of revenue.
Gross profit is revenue minus the cost of goods sold. Net profit is what remains after all expenses, including overheads, interest and tax.
The combined income of everyone in a household.
Tax charged on the income of individuals and businesses.
A tax collected by a business on a transaction and passed on to the government, such as {sales_tax}.
Goods a business holds to sell, and the materials used to make them. Also called stock.

US.def: Goods a business holds to sell, and the materials used to make them.

CA.def: Goods a business holds to sell, and the materials used to make them.

terms.def: Income earned from investments, such as interest, dividends, rent and capital gains.

A document a seller issues to a buyer listing the goods or services supplied, the amount due and the payment terms. If you're registered for {sales_tax}, it must meet {tax_authority_short} requirements.
A record of a transaction in the accounting system, showing the accounts debited and credited.
A measure a business tracks to see how well it is meeting its goals, such as gross margin or debtor days.
The balance of an account in the ledger at a point in time, after all recorded transactions.
Using borrowed money to buy assets or invest, which can magnify both gains and losses.
Anything a person or business owes, such as loans, supplier bills and tax.
A flexible loan that lets you borrow up to a set limit as needed, paying interest only on what you use.
Cash, and assets that can be quickly turned into cash without losing much value.
How easily assets can be turned into cash to meet short-term obligations.
A trust set up during a person's lifetime to hold and manage their assets, often used to avoid probate.
A sales charge or commission paid when buying or selling units in a mutual fund.
The difference between the selling price and the cost, usually shown as a percentage of the selling price.
Margin is profit as a percentage of the selling price. Markup is profit as a percentage of the cost.
The date a loan, bond or term deposit ends and the principal is repaid.
A loan secured against property, which the lender can claim if repayments aren't made.
An investment that pools money from many investors and is run by a professional fund manager.
When the amount owed on a loan is more than the current value of the asset it is secured against.
Income left after all expenses, allowances and taxes are deducted.
The profit left after all expenses, including overheads, interest and tax, are subtracted from revenue.
The total value of everything a person or business owns, minus everything it owes.
An asset that can't be quickly turned into cash without losing value, such as property or equipment.
A written promise to pay a set amount of money, either on demand or by a certain date.
Operating profit as a percentage of revenue. It shows how much of each sale is left after running costs.
Profit from a business's core operations, before interest and tax.
Contracts that give the holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell an asset at a set price by a set date.
Records of employees' pay, tax, {retirement_savings} and leave, which employers must keep and use for {payroll_reporting}.
The interest rate charged for each period of a loan, such as a monthly rate.
Investment in private companies, usually by funds that pool money from investors.
A report showing a business's income and expenses over a period, and the resulting profit or loss.

US.def: A report showing a business's income and expenses over a period, and the resulting profit or loss. Also called a profit and loss statement.

CA.def: A report showing a business's income and expenses over a period, and the resulting profit or loss. Also called a profit and loss statement.

terms.def: A contract setting out the price and conditions for buying an asset or business.
When a central bank creates money to buy financial assets, to lower interest rates and support the economy.
Current assets, excluding inventory, divided by current liabilities. It shows whether a business can pay its short-term debts.
A partial refund of an amount already paid.
A significant fall in economic activity lasting several months or more.
Replacing an existing loan with a new one, usually to get a better rate or different terms.
Net profit divided by total assets. It shows how efficiently a business uses its assets to make profit.
Net profit divided by owners' equity. It shows the return on the money the owners have invested.
The profit from an investment compared with what it cost, shown as a percentage.
The income a business earns from its normal activities, mainly selling goods or services.
The chance that an investment's return will be lower than expected, or that you will lose money.
Rules that protect a person or business from a penalty or liability if they meet set conditions.
A business owned and run by one person, with no legal separation between the owner and the business.
A licensed professional who buys and sells shares and other securities for investors.
A range of income taxed at a particular rate.
An amount that directly reduces the tax you owe, rather than your taxable income.
Delaying when tax is paid, for example by contributing to {retirement_savings}.
A report listing the balance of every general ledger account at a point in time, used to check debits equal credits.
Income that doesn't come from active work, such as rent, interest and dividends.
Debt that isn't backed by an asset the lender can take if you don't repay, such as most credit cards.
Investment in early-stage businesses with high growth potential, in exchange for a share of ownership.
Current assets minus current liabilities: the funds available to run the business day to day.
The period from the start of the current financial or calendar year up to today.
Supplies that don't attract {sales_tax}, such as most basic food. The business can still claim the {sales_tax} on its related costs.

CA.def: Supplies taxed at 0% GST/HST, such as basic groceries. The business can still claim input tax credits on related costs.

terms.def: A tax on most goods and services, collected by registered businesses and paid to {tax_authority} with each {sales_tax_return}.
The identifying number for your business, used with {tax_authority} and on invoices.
A deduction taken before adjusted gross income is worked out, such as some retirement contributions. It lowers AGI, which can affect other tax breaks.
A separate calculation that makes sure higher-income taxpayers with large deductions still pay at least a minimum amount of tax.
A system that stops company profits being taxed twice. Tax the company has paid passes to shareholders as credits they can use against their own tax.

AU.def: Credits for the tax a company has already paid, passed to shareholders with dividends. Shareholders use them to reduce their own tax, so profits aren't taxed twice.

NZ.def: Credits for the tax a company has already paid, passed to shareholders with dividends. Shareholders use them to reduce their own tax, so profits aren't taxed twice.

terms.def: Lodging a tax return online with the IRS, directly or through tax software or a preparer.
A federal tax on the value of a person's estate when they die, payable before it passes to beneficiaries. Only larger estates pay it.
A tax-advantaged account for medical costs, available to people on a high-deductible health plan. Unused money carries over each year.
Monthly housing costs (mortgage, property tax and insurance) as a share of gross monthly income. Lenders use it to judge whether you can afford a home loan.
A tax on a person's estate when they die, on the value above a tax-free threshold. Some gifts and transfers, such as to a spouse or civil partner, can be exempt.
Tax on gifts and inheritances above a tax-free threshold. The threshold depends on the relationship between the giver and the person receiving.
A local tax on the value of land and buildings, used to fund community services such as schools, roads and emergency services.
Charges a local council sets on property owners to fund local services such as roads, rubbish collection and parks.
A tax on homes collected by the local council to pay for local services. The amount depends on the property's valuation band.
An annual tax on residential property, based on the property's market value band, collected by Revenue.
A retirement account you pay into with after-tax money. Growth is tax-free and qualifying withdrawals in retirement are tax-free too.
A retirement account where contributions may be tax-deductible. Tax is paid when the money is withdrawn in retirement.
An IRA that lets you invest in a wider range of assets, such as property or private businesses, with stricter rules on how you deal with them.
A company that elects to pass its income, losses and credits through to shareholders for federal tax, so the business itself generally isn't taxed on its profit.
Extra forms filed with a federal tax return to report particular income and deductions, such as Schedule C for a sole proprietor's business profit.
Social Security and Medicare tax paid by people who work for themselves, on top of income tax.
A personal loan given on your credit history and signature alone, with no asset as security.
Tax owed on goods bought from outside your state without sales tax, when they are used in your state.
Income that the law lets you leave out of gross income, so it isn't taxed, such as some employer-provided benefits.
A workplace plan, such as a 401(k), where employees save part of their pay for retirement before tax, often with an employer match.
Extra payments for work-related costs or conditions, such as tools, travel, meals or working in difficult conditions.
Paid time off each year for employees to rest or take a holiday.
Pay an employee was owed for an earlier period but didn't receive, such as from an underpayment or a backdated pay rise.
An employee's standard rate of pay, before overtime, bonuses, allowances or benefits.
Extra pay on top of normal wages, usually at the employer's discretion as a reward or incentive. It is usually taxed like ordinary pay.
Someone employed on an as-needed basis with no firm commitment to ongoing hours. They are usually paid by the hour.
Payroll software run online, so pay runs, records and payslips can be reached from anywhere with a login.
Pay linked to results, usually a percentage of the sales an employee makes.
A person in business on their own account who is paid to do a job, rather than employed. They handle their own tax and aren't on the payroll.

US.def: A self-employed person paid to do a job rather than employed. No tax is withheld from their pay; they are usually reported on Form 1099-NEC.

CA.def: A self-employed person paid to do a job rather than employed. They aren't on the payroll and handle their own CPP and income tax.

terms.def: Paying wages straight into an employee's bank account instead of by cheque or cash.
A person employed under a contract of employment, who works under the employer's direction and is paid through payroll.
A person or business that employs staff and is responsible for paying them and meeting the related tax and employment obligations.
The agreement between employer and employee setting out duties, pay, hours and other terms.
Non-cash benefits an employer gives staff on top of pay, such as a work car or health insurance. Some are taxed.

UK.def: Non-cash benefits an employer gives staff on top of pay, such as a company car or private medical insurance. Most are taxable and reported to HMRC.

IE.def: Non-cash benefits an employer gives staff on top of pay, such as a company car. Most are taxed through payroll.

terms.def: A legal order requiring an employer to deduct money from an employee's pay and send it to a creditor or agency.
Total pay for a period before tax and any other deductions.
The time an employee is required to be at work or on duty, used to calculate pay and entitlements.
The lowest hourly rate an employer may legally pay. Rates are set by law and reviewed regularly.

AU.def: The lowest pay rate for employees not covered by an award or agreement, reviewed each year by the Fair Work Commission. Most employees are paid under an award instead.

terms.def: What an employee receives after tax and all other deductions. Also called take-home pay.
Bringing a new employee into the business: paperwork, payroll set-up, training and introductions.
Hours worked beyond an employee's normal hours. Depending on the law or agreement, it may be paid at a higher rate.
The span of time each pay covers, such as a week, fortnight or month.
The amount an employee is paid per hour, per period or per year before deductions.
A record given to employees each payday showing gross pay, deductions, net pay and leave balances.
A statement given with each pay showing gross pay, deductions and net pay for the period and the year to date.
Paying a business's employees, including working out pay, deductions and tax, and reporting to the authorities. Also the list of employees and what they are paid.
Using an outside provider to run the business's payroll, including pay runs and reporting.
Repaying an employee for work costs they paid themselves, such as travel. Genuine reimbursements usually aren't taxed as pay.
Paying amounts withheld from employees' pay, such as income tax, to the tax authority.

CA.def: Sending the CPP contributions, EI premiums and income tax withheld from employees' pay, plus the employer's share, to the CRA by the due date.

terms.def: A fixed amount of pay for a year, paid in regular instalments, rather than by the hour.
A payment to an employee whose job ends, often based on length of service.
A payment to an employee whose job is no longer needed. Minimum amounts are set by law in some cases, based on age and length of service.
Time off work because of illness or injury. Whether it is paid, and how much, depends on the law and the employment agreement.

AU.def: Paid leave when an employee is sick or injured, or needs to care for a family or household member. Minimum amounts are set by the National Employment Standards.

terms.def: A public holiday set by law. Employees who work it, or have it off, may be entitled to particular pay.
Money customers give staff on top of the bill. Tips are generally taxable income for the employee.
Pay for work, usually worked out on hours or days worked.
Income that tax is worked out on, after allowable deductions.
A legal document setting minimum pay rates and conditions for employees in an industry or occupation.
The form businesses lodge with the ATO to report and pay GST, PAYG withholding and other tax obligations.
An extra percentage on a casual employee's hourly rate, paid instead of paid leave and other entitlements permanent staff receive.
A way of giving employees shares or options in the company they work for, often with special tax rules.
The main federal law setting workplace rights, including the National Employment Standards and the system of awards.
The government agency that gives free advice on pay and workplace rights and enforces the Fair Work Act.
The end-of-year summary of an employee's pay, tax withheld and super, available in myGov once the employer finalises it through Single Touch Payroll.
A statement some businesses lodge with the ATO to report and pay PAYG withholding or instalments when they don't lodge a BAS for that period.
An extra amount, often 17.5%, paid on annual leave under many awards and agreements.
Extra paid leave for employees who have worked for the same employer for a long time. The rules come from state and territory laws.
The minimum entitlements for employees in the national system, such as maximum weekly hours, leave and notice of termination.
Leave for employees after the birth or adoption of a child. Government-funded Parental Leave Pay may be paid through the employer's payroll.
Tax an employer takes out of employees' pay and sends to the ATO.
A state and territory tax on employers whose total wages are above a threshold. It is paid by the employer, not taken from employees' pay.
Reporting each pay run's wages, tax withheld and super to the ATO from payroll software.
Retirement savings. Employers must pay a set percentage of most employees' ordinary earnings into their super fund.
The minimum super contribution employers must pay for eligible employees. Late or missed payments attract the super guarantee charge.
A personal reference number issued by the ATO. Employees give it to employers on a TFN declaration so the right tax is withheld.
Amounts paid when employment ends, such as unused leave, pay in lieu of notice and redundancy pay. Some parts are taxed differently.
Insurance employers must hold to cover employees' wages and medical costs if they are injured or become ill because of work. Run by each state and territory.
Payments to the Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC) that fund cover for injuries. Employees' earners' levy is deducted through PAYE; employers pay a work levy.
A paid day off an employee earns for working on a public holiday that would otherwise be a working day for them.
Tax on an employer's contributions to an employee's KiwiSaver or other super fund, deducted before the contribution is paid.
The pay and deduction details employers file with Inland Revenue after each payday.
A tax employers pay on non-cash benefits given to staff, such as private use of a work vehicle.
Pay for annual holidays and public holidays under the Holidays Act.
The year income tax is worked out on, usually 1 April to 31 March.
The number Inland Revenue gives to people and organisations for tax. Employees give it to their employer on a tax code declaration.
A voluntary retirement savings scheme. Members contribute a chosen percentage of their pay, and employers must also contribute for eligible employees.
The government pension paid to eligible New Zealanders from age 65, funded from general taxes. Nothing is deducted through payroll for it, and it is separate from KiwiSaver.
The government's investment fund that helps pay for NZ Super in the future. Individuals and employers don't contribute to it.
A workplace or other registered retirement scheme besides KiwiSaver. Employer contributions to it are taxed with ESCT, as KiwiSaver contributions are.
A break from KiwiSaver contributions for a set time, approved by Inland Revenue. Formerly called a contributions holiday.
When some public holidays fall on a weekend that isn't a working day for the employee, the holiday moves to the following Monday (or Tuesday).
A unique number that identifies a business in New Zealand, used to share its key details with government and other businesses.
A day the employee would normally have worked. It decides whether they get paid for a public holiday and earn a day in lieu.
Pay as you earn: income tax and the ACC earners' levy that employers deduct from employees' pay and send to Inland Revenue.
Filing employment information with Inland Revenue within two working days of each payday.
The minimum share of an employee's pay that must be left after certain deductions, such as child support, are taken.
A notice from Inland Revenue telling an employer or bank to take money owed by a taxpayer, such as unpaid tax or child support, and pay it to Inland Revenue.
A payroll run for an employee paid from overseas while working in New Zealand, so the right PAYE is reported and paid here.
A code an employee chooses on a tax code declaration so the right amount of PAYE is deducted, for example for a main or secondary job.
The legal duty for employers to put eligible workers into a workplace pension and pay in at least a minimum contribution.
A report to HMRC to claim reductions, such as statutory pay recovery or Employment Allowance, or to say no employees were paid.
A reduction in the employer's National Insurance bill each year for eligible businesses.
The report sent to HMRC on or before each payday with employees' pay and deductions, under Real Time Information.
HM Revenue & Customs, the UK tax authority.
HMRC's programme requiring businesses to keep digital records and file returns, such as VAT, using compatible software.
Contributions paid by employees and employers on earnings, which count towards the State Pension and some benefits.
The legal minimum hourly pay for workers above a set age. Rates change each April.
The form given to an employee when they leave, showing their pay and tax to date for the new employer.
The year-end summary of an employee's pay and tax for the tax year, given by 31 May.
The form employers use to report employees' benefits in kind and expenses to HMRC after the tax year, unless they are payrolled.
Pay As You Earn: the system employers use to deduct Income Tax and National Insurance from pay and send it to HMRC.
Reporting employees' pay and deductions to HMRC every time they are paid, rather than once a year.
Pay for eligible employees on maternity leave, paid through payroll. Employers can reclaim most or all of it from HMRC.
The minimum sick pay employers must pay eligible employees who are too ill to work.
The code HMRC issues for each job or pension, telling the employer how much tax-free pay to allow before deducting Income Tax.
A legal employment status between employee and self-employed. Workers have some rights, such as the minimum wage and holiday pay, but not all of an employee's.
A pension the employer sets up for staff, with contributions from the employee's pay and from the employer.
Pay As You Earn: the system employers use to deduct income tax, PRSI and USC from pay and send it to Revenue.
The real-time system under which employers report each employee's pay and deductions to Revenue on or before every payday.
Pay Related Social Insurance: contributions paid by employees and employers on earnings, which fund social welfare benefits and pensions.
A tax on gross income, charged at rising rates on income above a threshold, deducted through payroll.
The tax credits and rate band details Revenue gives the employer for each employee, used to work out their tax.
Amounts that reduce the tax a person pays, such as the personal and employee tax credits.
Revenue's end-of-year summary of an employee's pay and deductions, available in myAccount.
The national retirement savings scheme that eligible employees are put into automatically, with contributions from employee, employer and the State.
An employer-sponsored retirement plan where employees save part of their pay before tax (or after tax in a Roth 401(k)), often with an employer match.
Paying employees every two weeks, which gives 26 paydays a year.
A plan that lets employees choose benefits, such as health insurance, and pay for them before tax.
Paid time off given instead of overtime pay. Private employers generally can't use it in place of overtime for non-exempt staff.
The federal tax ID the IRS gives a business, used on payroll tax filings.
The Employee Retirement Income Security Act: federal law setting standards for most private-sector retirement and health plans.
An employee not entitled to overtime under the Fair Labor Standards Act, usually salaried and in a qualifying role.
An employee entitled to overtime pay for hours over 40 in a workweek under the Fair Labor Standards Act.
Social Security and Medicare taxes. Employers withhold the employee's share from pay and pay a matching share.
Federal unemployment tax, paid by employers only, which funds unemployment benefits along with state programs.
An account employees pay into before tax to cover medical or dependent care costs. Most unused money is lost at the end of the plan year.
The year-end form showing an employee's wages and taxes withheld, given to the employee and filed with the Social Security Administration.
The form employees fill in so their employer withholds the right amount of federal income tax.
The form used to report payments of $600 or more to independent contractors.
Health insurance with a higher deductible and lower premiums. It is needed to open a health savings account.
Pay based on the number of items produced or tasks completed rather than hours worked.
A simplified employee pension: a retirement plan where the employer, including a self-employed person, contributes to IRAs for each eligible employee.
The number the Social Security Administration gives each person, used for employment and tax records.
State unemployment tax, paid by employers (and in a few states employees) to fund state unemployment benefits.
Tax an employer deducts from an employee's pay and sends to the government on their behalf.
A public pension plan. Employees and employers each contribute on earnings up to a yearly maximum. Quebec has its own plan (QPP).
The federal agency that administers tax, including payroll deductions, across Canada. Quebec collects its own provincial income tax.
A federal program that gives temporary income to eligible workers who lose their job or are on leave, such as parental leave. Employees and employers pay premiums.
The minimum rules for wages, hours, leave and termination set by federal, provincial or territorial law.
Earnings that EI premiums are worked out on, up to a yearly maximum.
Quebec's public pension plan, which replaces the CPP for people working in Quebec.
The form an employer issues to Service Canada when an employee has an interruption of earnings, used to decide EI benefits.
A retirement savings account. Contributions can be deducted from income, and tax is paid when money is withdrawn.
An RRSP an employer sets up for staff, with contributions taken from pay and sometimes matched by the employer.
The nine-digit number Service Canada gives each person to work and receive government benefits.
The year-end slip showing an employee's pay and deductions, filed with the CRA and given to the employee.
The form employees fill in so their employer deducts the right amount of income tax.
Pay for vacation time, or a percentage of earnings paid instead, as set by employment standards.

US.def: Pay for vacation time an employer offers. Federal law doesn't require paid vacation; it depends on the employer's policy and some state laws.

terms.def: Permission for someone who isn't a citizen or permanent resident to work in Canada.
